items.title: Baseline Digital Fraud Reporting and Customer Notification Advisory
items.content:
circular_id: RBI-BASE-2025-001
title: Baseline Digital Fraud Reporting and Customer Notification Advisory
category: Digital Fraud / Reporting
issue_date: 2025-04-15
regulator: Reserve Bank of India
effective_from: 2025-05-01

The Reserve Bank of India advises all scheduled commercial banks to maintain a baseline digital fraud reporting process for internet banking, mobile banking, card-not-present payments, UPI-linked transactions, and other cyber-enabled payment channels. This advisory establishes the earlier control expectation against which future accelerated fraud reporting circulars may be assessed by bank compliance teams.

Banks must record every confirmed or suspected digital fraud incident in a central incident register within 24 hours of detection by the branch, fraud monitoring team, contact centre, or digital channels operations team. The register should capture customer identifier, transaction reference, fraud category, detection timestamp, preliminary loss estimate, affected channel, reporting owner, and current containment status. The Fraud Risk Department should review the register daily and escalate unresolved high-value cases to the Compliance Office.

Banks should notify affected customers through registered mobile number, email, branch communication, or contact centre callback when fraud impact is confirmed. The notification should describe the transaction under review, customer reporting options, expected support process, and grievance escalation channel. The customer notification process may be completed within 24 hours after internal confirmation of fraud impact, unless a law enforcement hold or operational risk exception is approved.

The Compliance Office must submit a consolidated fraud incident summary to senior management and internal compliance forums on a monthly basis. The summary should include fraud trend, impacted channels, recovery status, customer complaints, regulatory reporting status, and corrective actions. Regulatory reporting to RBI or law enforcement should follow the bank's existing fraud reporting SOP and applicable materiality thresholds.

Banks must retain incident register entries, customer notification proof, investigation notes, and approval records for audit review. Internal Audit may sample fraud records during periodic compliance testing. This advisory does not mandate four-hour reporting, customer impact metadata in every regulatory submission, or automated evidence hash preservation. Banks are expected to update this baseline when RBI issues a stricter circular.

items.title: Mule Account KYC and AML Monitoring Advisory
items.content:
circular_id: RBI-BASE-2025-002
title: Mule Account KYC and AML Monitoring Advisory
category: KYC / AML / Mule Account Monitoring
issue_date: 2025-07-10
regulator: Reserve Bank of India
effective_from: 2025-08-01

The Reserve Bank of India advises banks to strengthen baseline controls for mule account identification, enhanced KYC review, AML monitoring, and branch-level escalation of suspicious account activity. This advisory is intended to help banks detect accounts used as pass-through channels for fraud proceeds, unusual transaction velocity, or rapid beneficiary churn.

Banks must maintain transaction monitoring scenarios for accounts that show sudden cash-out behaviour, high-frequency inward credits followed by immediate withdrawals, repeated use of newly added beneficiaries, unusual device or IP overlap, and account activity inconsistent with the stated customer profile. Fraud Risk Department, KYC / AML Compliance, and Branch Operations should jointly review mule account alerts generated by core banking, AML systems, and digital channel monitoring tools.

Banks should conduct enhanced KYC verification for accounts flagged as suspected mule accounts. The review should include customer identity information, occupation and income profile, recent address or mobile changes, linked account relationships, beneficial owner details where applicable, and prior suspicious transaction reports. Branch Operations should contact the customer where appropriate and record the outcome in the KYC review tracker.

Suspicious mule account cases must be escalated to the KYC / AML Compliance team for review. The team should decide whether to freeze activity, file a suspicious transaction report, monitor the account, or close the case with documented justification. Cases involving digital fraud proceeds should also be shared with the Fraud Risk Department for recovery and customer impact assessment.

Banks must preserve mule account alert records, KYC documents, escalation notes, account freeze approvals, suspicious transaction review notes, and branch customer contact proof for audit. Monthly review of unresolved mule account alerts should be presented to the Compliance Office and Risk Management. This baseline advisory does not mandate daily branch escalation packs, device-overlap scoring, or regulator-ready weekly evidence bundles unless a later RBI circular introduces those requirements.

items.title: Cyber Incident Evidence Retention and Audit Trail Directive
items.content:
circular_id: RBI-BASE-2025-003
title: Cyber Incident Evidence Retention and Audit Trail Directive
category: Cyber Incident / Evidence Retention / Audit
issue_date: 2025-09-05
regulator: Reserve Bank of India
effective_from: 2025-10-01

The Reserve Bank of India directs banks to maintain baseline cybersecurity incident records, evidence retention controls, Security Operations Center escalation procedures, and audit trail preservation for technology and digital banking incidents. The directive applies to internet banking, mobile banking, payment gateways, internal banking applications, infrastructure systems, cloud workloads, and third-party technology services used for regulated banking operations.

Banks must log cybersecurity events that indicate unauthorized access, malware infection, data leakage, privilege misuse, payment channel compromise, distributed denial of service, credential theft, or suspicious administrative activity. The Security Operations Center should register each incident with detection timestamp, affected asset, impacted channel, severity, initial containment action, ticket owner, and escalation status. Critical events should be escalated to Cybersecurity / IT Security leadership and the Technology Risk team within 24 hours.

Banks should preserve relevant evidence for every material cybersecurity incident. Evidence may include SIEM alerts, firewall logs, endpoint telemetry, identity and access logs, application logs, transaction monitoring extracts, incident tickets, forensic images where available, and containment approval records. Evidence must be stored in a controlled repository with access logs and chain-of-custody notes. Audit records should be maintained for at least five years or longer where legal, regulatory, or investigation requirements apply.

The Compliance Office, Cybersecurity Wing, IT Vertical, and Internal Audit should coordinate periodic review of incident closure quality. Internal Audit may verify that incident tickets contain evidence references, root cause summary, customer impact assessment if applicable, remediation status, and management sign-off. Material incidents should be summarized for senior management and risk committees in the regular cyber resilience review.

This directive does not require automated evidence hash generation for every incident, four-hour external reporting, or mandatory CERT-In escalation for all low-severity events. Later circulars or CERT-In directions may impose stricter timelines, reporting formats, evidence artifacts, or regulator notification procedures. Banks must compare new circulars against this directive before updating the cyber incident response SOP.

items.title: Master Direction on Outsourcing of Information Technology Services
items.category: IT Outsourcing / Third-Party Risk / Cloud / SOC
items.content:
circular_id: RBI-REF-2023-IT-OUTSOURCING
title: Master Direction on Outsourcing of Information Technology Services
category: IT Outsourcing / Third-Party Risk / Cloud / SOC
issue_date: 2023-04-10
regulator: Reserve Bank of India
effective_from: 2023-10-01
status: Archived / Bank-provided public reference
source_type: Public regulatory reference

This bank-provided public reference summarizes the Reserve Bank of India Master Direction on Outsourcing of Information Technology Services for use as an approved policy reference in offline compliance analysis.

Regulated entities shall maintain a Board-approved IT outsourcing policy covering governance, accountability, risk assessment, due diligence, contracting, monitoring, business continuity, data protection, audit, reporting, and exit management for outsourced IT services.

The Board and Senior Management shall retain ultimate responsibility for outsourced IT activities and shall ensure that outsourcing arrangements do not reduce the regulated entity's obligations to customers or regulators. The IT Function, Risk Management, Compliance Department, Legal Department, Business Verticals, Procurement and Vendor Management, Cybersecurity Wing, and Internal Audit shall have documented roles for implementation and oversight.

Regulated entities must maintain a central inventory of outsourced IT services. The inventory shall include service provider name, service scope, business owner, technology owner, data handled, customer impact level, criticality rating, contract expiry date, subcontractor dependency, concentration risk, and exit dependency.

Before entering or renewing material IT outsourcing arrangements, regulated entities shall perform service provider due diligence covering financial soundness, operational capability, cyber security controls, data protection controls, legal risk, reputational risk, concentration risk, subcontractor dependency, business continuity readiness, and ability to comply with regulatory requirements.

Every material IT outsourcing agreement must be legally binding and must include service standards, roles and responsibilities, data confidentiality, customer data protection, access to records, audit rights, RBI inspection access, incident reporting obligations, subcontractor approval controls, business continuity requirements, termination rights, exit strategy, data portability, secure deletion, and transition support.

Regulated entities shall monitor and control outsourced activities through service level reporting, risk reviews, incident records, contract reviews, audit observations, closure tracking, and periodic reporting to Senior Management. Outsourcing arrangements shall be subject to a risk management framework, including concentration risk assessment and ongoing control testing.

Service providers must report cyber incidents and material service disruptions without undue delay so that the regulated entity can meet applicable regulatory reporting timelines. Incident response processes shall integrate service provider escalation, evidence preservation, containment actions, and senior management reporting.

Regulated entities shall ensure subcontractor controls, including prior approval, risk assessment, confidentiality obligations, data location controls, audit access, service continuity, and accountability for subcontracted activities.

Regulated entities shall test business continuity and disaster recovery arrangements for material outsourced IT services at least annually. Evidence of BCP and DRP testing, gaps observed, corrective actions, recovery objectives, cyber resilience testing, and management approvals shall be retained for audit review.

Cross-border outsourcing shall include country risk assessment, data access controls, regulatory access assurance, customer confidentiality safeguards, legal enforceability, incident reporting arrangements, and exit or transition options.

For cloud service providers, regulated entities shall ensure cloud governance, data classification, access control, privileged access monitoring, encryption, logging, monitoring, disaster recovery, cyber resilience, data portability, secure deletion during exit, and control over customer or confidential information.

For outsourced Security Operations Centre services, regulated entities shall maintain oversight over alert rules, log sources, logs, metadata, escalation workflows, incident response integration, SOC effectiveness reviews, evidence retention, and periodic review of managed security service performance.

Regulated entities shall conduct periodic audits of service providers and maintain evidence of audit reports, risk reviews, SLA monitoring, incident records, contract reviews, access reviews, management sign-offs, and closure of observations. RBI and the regulated entity must retain inspection and audit access to outsourced IT arrangements.

Regulated entities must maintain an exit strategy and transition plan for material outsourced IT services, including continuity arrangements, data return, secure deletion, replacement provider readiness, transition responsibilities, and management approval.
